contents:
Weekly summary This week I extended CIT from storing individual incidents to connecting them to users. I also introduced DAO interfaces, prepared an isolated database test setup and added an incident service for validation and application operations. This summary covers the work available through 3 October; the week is still in progress.
What I implemented Added a User entity with an automatically generated ID, a required name and a required, unique email address. Linked each incident to a reporter through a required, unidirectional ManyToOne relationship. Several incidents can refer to the same user through reported_by_id. Added UserDAO methods for creating users and finding a user by email. Added a parameterised JPQL query in IncidentDAO to find incidents by reporter ID, ordered by incident ID. Introduced IUserDAO and IIncidentDAO to describe the available persistence operations. Incident CRUD remains in the DAO layer, with transactions and rollback for writes. Updated the manual example in Main to connect an incident to a stored user, retrieve it and list incidents belonging to that reporter. Added IncidentService, which depends on the DAO interfaces. It supports creating incidents, finding one or all incidents, listing by reporter, changing status and deleting incidents. The service rejects blank titles and reporter emails, missing severity, descriptions longer than 2,000 characters, invalid IDs and null status values. It looks up an existing reporter before creation and throws an exception when a required user or incident cannot be found. New incidents retain the entity’s default OPEN status.
Testing progress I added JUnit and Testcontainers support, plus a PostgreSQL test container and a Hibernate test configuration using create-drop. The current test checks that the container is running and the EntityManagerFactory is open.
This is the foundation for database integration tests. There are no assertions yet for incident CRUD, reporter filtering or service validation. The test suite was inspected, but was not executed for this report, so this entry does not claim a passing test run. The local move of HibernateTestConfig into app.config is present in the working tree but has not yet been committed.
Technical choices and learning points The reporter relationship connects the JPA model to the project domain: an incident belongs to a reporting user. It is kept unidirectional, without cascade operations, so the service finds an existing user before persisting an incident.
DAO interfaces separate the operation contracts from their database implementations. The service adds a place for input checks and application behaviour, while DAO methods handle persistence. This also provides a basis for testing the service independently later.
The test container gives the tests a separate database. Starting that database is only the first step; meaningful tests still need to assert the data and behaviour of each operation.
Connection to the course This week’s implementation applies JPA Relations through the reporter relationship, DAO interfaces and JPQL queries. It also starts the testing work with an isolated database setup and prepares validation for a future REST layer.
The teaching schedule covers REST & Test in week 40, but CIT does not yet expose REST endpoints or contain REST Assured endpoint tests. The log records the project’s actual progress rather than treating all course topics as completed features.
Open points and next steps Add database tests for CRUD, user lookup and filtering incidents by reporter. Add service tests for valid input, invalid input and missing records. Correct the manual example: the email used to look up the sample user differs from the email used to create it, so repeated runs can attempt a duplicate insert. Verify existing database rows against the required status, severity and reporter fields; no completed migration is documented. Build the REST layer and document its endpoints once the current behaviour has been checked. Based on CIT commits 823b969, 8d9466d and 4b5142a, together with the local source and test files inspected on 3 October 2026.

contents:
Weekly summary This week I established the persistence foundation of the backend. The recorded implementation work is from 18–19 September.
What I implemented I worked on the foundation of SM3-CIT, my Cyber Incident Tracker project, using Java, JPA/Hibernate and PostgreSQL.
Set up the project packages and an Incident entity with an ID, title and description. Implemented an IncidentDAO to create, find, list, update and delete incidents. Used database transactions with commit and rollback for operations that change data. Added a small program in Main to manually try out the CRUD flow using a test incident. I confirmed that the CRUD flow worked before moving on to status and severity. This was a manual check, rather than an automated test suite.
Challenges and lessons learned One important distinction was between the Java entity and the database table: JPQL queries use the entity name Incident, while the table is named incidents.
I also worked through how persist() saves a new entity and merge() copies changes into an entity managed by the current EntityManager. Each DAO method opens and closes its own EntityManager.
Status and severity The next step was to make the data model more useful for tracking security incidents. I added enums for:
Status: OPEN, INVESTIGATING, CONTAINED, RESOLVED. Severity: LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL. The entity stores the enum names as text. New Java objects start with status OPEN and severity MEDIUM.
Open issue Existing database rows need attention before the new required fields can be used safely. Java default values do not automatically fill those fields in rows already stored in the database. Handling that change and checking the updated model remained the next step at the end of this week.
Next steps Handle status and severity for existing database rows. Run the CRUD flow again with the updated fields. Add automated DAO tests after the manual flow is working. Connection to the course This work applies the JPA Basics material: entity mapping, Lombok, CRUD, EntityManager, transactions and JPQL. Although the semester schedule places SP1 in week 38, this entry records the actual CIT work completed during that calendar week.
Retrospective weekly summary based on the existing development notes and CIT commit ea16dd9 (19 September 2026).

contents:
Cyber Incident Tracker SM3-CIT is my third-semester Cyber Incident Tracker project. I am building the backend in Java, using JPA/Hibernate and PostgreSQL. This portfolio documents the implementation and its connection to the course through the backend exam in early November 2026.
Current implementation As of 3 October, the project contains incident CRUD, status and severity enums, users and a required relationship between incidents and their reporters. DAO interfaces define persistence operations, and JPQL supports finding users by email and incidents by reporter. An incident service adds validation and application operations on top of the DAOs.
The automated test setup uses JUnit and a PostgreSQL Testcontainer. Its current test checks database startup; CRUD and service behaviour still need automated coverage. No test run was performed for this report.
REST endpoints, external API integration, concurrency features, authentication and deployment are not yet documented as implemented in the inspected CIT source. These remain later backend work.
Weekly development log Each entry collects the whole week’s implemented work, technical choices, testing progress and next steps. Further work in the same week is added to that entry. Weeks follow the actual project history, with a separate explanation of their connection to the teaching topics.
The available history documents work in weeks 38 and 40. There is no separately evidenced implementation for week 39, so no progress entry has been invented for that week. The week 40 summary is current through 3 October.
